summaries.gardner: Valero fits Rule Breaker investing poorly: it is the leader of a mature, century-old refining industry rather than an emerging one, and it has no hard-to-copy innovation edge. Its only Gardner-like traits are strong price momentum (up about 176% over 52 weeks to $444.71) and some commentators calling it expensive versus the $406.58 average target.
summaries.buffett: Buffett would like that Valero is simple, large, run by disciplined operators and returns most cash to owners (diluted shares down from 407M in 2020 to 294M in Q2 2026). But earnings are highly cyclical (a $1,421M loss in 2020, $11,528M profit in 2022, $2,348M in 2025), it has no pricing power, and at about 18.5x trailing earnings near a record margin peak there is no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would see an understandable but commodity business whose returns depend on crack spreads it cannot control, with only a modest scale and complexity advantage. Inverting, the ways it can disappoint (margin normalisation, EV-driven demand decline, regulation) are numerous, so it is not the kind of wonderful business at a fair price he favoured.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Valero as a classic cyclical, and his rule is to buy cyclicals when earnings are depressed and P/Es look high, and to be wary when earnings peak. With record 2026 refining margins, Q2 2026 EPS of $12.62 versus $2.28 a year earlier and consensus expecting EPS to fall in 2027, the stock looks late in the cycle, though buybacks and a low forward P/E keep it on a cyclical investor's radar.
summaries.fisher: Valero scores weakly on Fisher's growth points: revenue has not grown over five years, R&D is minor and its fuels are undifferentiated. It does score on management depth, safety and operating excellence (record 97.5% mechanical availability in 2025) and on honest, shareholder-friendly capital allocation.
summaries.graham: Valero passes several of Graham's defensive tests (large size, a dividend paid every year since 1997, current ratio of 1.64) but fails others: it lost money in 2020, FY2025 EPS of $7.57 was below 2015's $7.99, and the price is about 32x its 2023-2025 average EPS with P/E times P/B near 97. It does not meet the defensive investor's valuation criteria.
summaries.thiel: Valero is the opposite of a Zero to One company: it competes in a crowded commodity market with no proprietary technology and no monopoly, only economies of scale and the fact that new US refineries are rarely built. Its durability rests on the slow decline of fossil fuels rather than on a unique secret.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on durable growth businesses riding major platform shifts, bought at reasonable prices with attention to cost discipline. Valero has cost discipline and strong cash returns but no secular growth and depends on commodity spreads, so it fits his approach only as a tactical, macro-driven trade.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and rising estimates driven by a macro catalyst, and Valero has both today: the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption pushed refining margins to records, Q2 2026 EPS beat consensus by over 20% and 2026 estimates have been raised repeatedly. The risk is timing, since consensus already sees earnings declining in 2027 and 2028.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would reject Valero: gross margin is only about 4.4% (FY2025), returns on capital swing widely with the cycle, and there is no consistent high return or growth to compound. It fails his 'good company' test regardless of price.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Valero looks decent today: trailing operating income of about $10,011M against an enterprise value of roughly $134 billion gives an earnings yield near 7.5%, and pre-tax return on capital is high at peak margins. But both figures are inflated by a cyclical peak, and on FY2025 numbers (operating income $3,181M) it would rank poorly.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs an extraordinary business, talented and honest management, and the ability to reinvest at high rates. Valero has capable, honest management but a commodity business with few high-return reinvestment opportunities, so it returns cash rather than compounding it.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for low-risk, high-uncertainty bets on simple businesses in temporary distress. Valero is simple and financially sound (net debt-to-capitalization 11% at June 30, 2026), but it is at a cyclical high rather than in distress, so the downside is meaningful and the Dhandho 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' set-up is absent.
summaries.wood: Valero does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation framework at all: it refines fossil fuels, which ARK sees as a business threatened by electric vehicles and energy storage. Its renewable diesel and SAF lines are incremental rather than exponential platforms.
summaries.ackman: Ackman seeks simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and high barriers to entry. Valero is simple and generates strong cash in good years, but its earnings are not predictable and its barriers are limited to scale and permitting, so it fits only partly.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model does not apply: Valero's lower costs are not passed to customers to build an ever-widening moat, since fuel prices are set by global markets. Its long-term position is unlikely to be clearly stronger in 10 to 20 years as fuel demand in its core markets plateaus.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets and technologies creating new demand; Valero operates in a large but mature market with no technology-driven growth. It is a solid operator of essential infrastructure, not a venture-style opportunity.
summaries.nash: Valero fails most of Tom Nash's screens: it is a commodity processor, carries more debt and finance leases ($11,349M) than cash ($7,874M), has a trailing operating margin of about 7%, and his DCF on 3-year averages gives roughly $169 per share versus $444.71. It scores well on momentum, short interest, institutional ownership and earnings beats, but its 13-category score of about 70 is below his 75 threshold.

momentum.evidence: The share price rose about 176% over 52 weeks to $444.71 at the Oct 16, 2026 close, near its 52-week high of $461.52, far ahead of the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Lane Riggs is a respected 37-year refining veteran and institutions own about 86% of the shares, but there is no famous strategic partner beyond the Darling Ingredients Diamond Green Diesel JV.

g6.evidence: The price of $444.71 is above the $406.58 average analyst target and 9 of 20 analysts rate it Hold with 2 Strong Sell, but most commentators frame it as a cyclical peak rather than a high-growth stock being called overvalued.

simple.evidence: Valero buys crude oil and sells gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, plus ethanol and renewable diesel; refining was 95% of FY2025 revenue.

integrity.evidence: Valero sticks to a stated payout framework (59% of adjusted operating cash flow returned in Q2 2026), has kept debt low and has been an Extel Most Honored Company nine straight years for its executive team and investor relations.

b6.evidence: Valero has avoided large acquisitions in recent years, idled its loss-making Benicia refinery in April 2026 and kept 2025 capital investments to about $1.9 billion including turnarounds.

roic.evidence: Pre-tax return on capital was roughly 31% on trailing operating income of $10,011M at June 2026 but only about 10% on FY2025 operating income of $3,181M, so returns are high but not consistent.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow after all capital investments was $3,941M in 2025 versus net income of $2,348M, and about $9,291M over the twelve months to June 2026 versus $7,212M of net income.

b10.evidence: Valero's market value rose from about $31 billion in October 2021 to about $128 billion while it bought back heavily, but the gain owes much to the refining cycle rather than reinvested earnings.

safety.evidence: A DCF on 3-year average growth and FCF margin gives about $169 per share, far below the $444.71 price, and the price is near a cyclical peak.

fairprice.evidence: At about 18.5x trailing EPS of $23.98 and peak-cycle margins, with consensus EPS expected to fall about 11% in 2027, the price is not cheap for a no-growth commodity business.

mu5.evidence: The balance sheet is strong (net debt-to-capitalization 11%), but earnings can collapse with crack spreads, as in 2020's loss, and EVs, regulation and new overseas refineries pose long-term risks.

reinvest.evidence: Valero spends only about $2 billion a year on capital and returns most cash through dividends and buybacks because high-return refining expansion opportunities are scarce.

ly2.evidence: Valero is a textbook Lynch cyclical whose earnings rise and fall with refining margins.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E is about 18.5 while consensus expects EPS to decline in 2027 (from $52.57 to $46.74), so P/E is well above the growth rate.

runway.evidence: Revenue fell from $176,383M in 2022 to $122,687M in 2025, and US and European fuel demand is near a plateau, with only small renewable fuel growth.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 407M in 2020 to 294M in Q2 2026 through buybacks, but we found no evidence of open-market insider buying.

ly8.evidence: Refining is a boring niche, but Valero is followed by about 20 analysts and is widely owned by institutions.

fi2.evidence: Valero developed renewable diesel through Diamond Green Diesel and started neat SAF production at Port Arthur in late 2024, but its core products remain gasoline and diesel.

fi3.evidence: Valero does not report meaningful R&D spending; its new products come from capital projects such as DGD Port Arthur rather than research.

fi4.evidence: Fuels are sold on price into wholesale, branded and export channels; there is no evidence of unusual sales ability.

longterm.evidence: Management invests in long-life assets such as the $230M St. Charles FCC optimisation and SAF, but its priority is near-term cash returns to shareholders.

gr1.evidence: Valero had FY2025 revenue of $122,687M and a market value of about $128 billion.

ni10.evidence: Valero lost $1,421M attributable to stockholders in 2020.

gr4.evidence: Valero has paid dividends since 1997, about 29 years, and paid $4.52 per share in 2025.

eps10.evidence: FY2025 diluted EPS of $7.57 was below FY2015's $7.99, though trailing EPS to June 2026 of $23.98 is about three times higher.

gr6.evidence: Average diluted EPS for 2023-2025 was about $13.69, so $444.71 is roughly 32x average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 18.5 times a price-to-book of about 5.2 gives roughly 97, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Refining technology is widely licensed and Valero has no proprietary process ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: 2026 is an exceptionally strong moment for refiners because of the Iran conflict and record crack spreads, but that is cyclical timing rather than a lasting technology shift.

th3.evidence: Valero grew by buying existing refineries in a large mature market, not by dominating a small new one.

team.evidence: Management is experienced and operationally excellent (record safety and 97.5% mechanical availability in 2025) but not a world-class visionary founder team.

th5.evidence: Valero supplies about 7,000 branded outlets and has Gulf Coast docks and logistics to export fuels to Latin America and Europe.

durable.evidence: Fuel demand will persist for decades and new US refineries are rare, but EV adoption and policy may erode gasoline demand over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Refining is a well-understood business with many large competitors.

trend.evidence: Valero is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud computing; its exposure to the energy transition is limited to renewable diesel and SAF.

dr1.evidence: Q2 2026 EPS was $12.62 versus $2.28 a year earlier, and 2026 consensus EPS rose from $42.96 to about $53 between September and October 2026.

dr2.evidence: Consensus already expects revenue and EPS to decline in 2027 and 2028 as crack spreads normalise.

dr4.evidence: Supply disruptions from the Middle East conflict favour US refiners, but a weaker economy or demand destruction from high fuel prices could hurt.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on Oct 22 should reflect record July crack spreads, and the St. Charles FCC optimisation project was due to start up in Q3 2026.

dr7.evidence: With earnings near a cyclical peak and highly sensitive to oil-market events, conviction is not high enough for a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: FY2025 gross margin (revenue minus cost of sales) was about 4.4%, typical of a commodity processor.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $9,291M is roughly a 7% yield on a $131 billion market value, but at FY2025 FCF of $3,941M it would be about 3%.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $10,011M is about 7.5% of a roughly $134 billion enterprise value, but only about 2.4% using FY2025 operating income of $3,181M.

pa2.evidence: Refining is in a boom, not a setback, with record margins in 2026.

pa4.evidence: Low net debt makes bankruptcy unlikely, but buying at record margins risks a large, lasting price decline if the cycle turns.

wo1.evidence: Valero is not active in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Refining costs are driven by crude and energy prices, not by steep learning curves.

wo3.evidence: Valero combines refining, ethanol and renewable diesel, none of which are innovation platforms in Wood's sense.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable fuels market is mature and will not multiply in five years.

ac3.evidence: Valero's results swing with crude prices and crack spreads, from a $1,579M operating loss in 2020 to $15,690M operating income in 2022.

ns1.evidence: Fuel prices are set by global markets, so Valero does not pass scale savings to customers to widen a moat.

ns4.evidence: Gasoline demand in its core markets is expected to plateau or decline, so its position in 10-20 years is unlikely to be clearly stronger.

va2.evidence: Reliable, affordable transportation fuel is essential, and the 2026 supply shock showed how painful shortages are.

tn1.evidence: Valero is a traditional oil refiner rather than a company built for a new secular trend; renewable diesel and SAF were under 3% of FY2025 revenue.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Valero as a refiner, which is what it is and will remain.

tn3.evidence: Valero is a commodity processor whose earnings depend on oil and fuel prices, a zone Nash avoids.

tn9.evidence: Valero has more debt than cash and a trailing operating margin of about 7%, well below 20%.

tn11.evidence: Valero provides gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and renewable fuels that help drivers, airlines and businesses keep moving, and charges per gallon at market prices, winning on reliable supply and low cost.

tn13.evidence: Total about 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 10, operating margin 0, short interest (3.1%) 10, institutional ownership (86%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 10, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 0, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn18.evidence: Riggs has executed well operationally, but he has been CEO only since June 2023, is not a founder and we found no open-market share purchases.

tn22.evidence: Valero has $122,687M of revenue, solid profits and shrinks its share count through buybacks rather than issuing stock.

tn24.evidence: At about 14x trailing free cash flow the price implies sustained growth from peak-cycle cash flows, while revenue has fallen at about 11% a year over 2023-2025.
